question: What is the difference between let and var in Swift?
answer:
A `let` binding can be assigned exactly once; a `var` binding can be reassigned as often as you like.

• let — the binding is fixed after initialization. Initialization can still be deferred, so `let x: Int; if c { x = 1 } else { x = 2 }` is legal.
• var — the binding can be pointed at a new value at any time.

The interesting part is how this interacts with value and reference semantics:
• For a value type (struct, enum) `let` freezes the whole value — you cannot mutate its stored properties or call a `mutating` method on it.
• For a reference type (class) `let` freezes only the reference — the object's own `var` properties are still settable through it.

Idiomatic Swift is `let` by default; the compiler emits a warning when a `var` is never mutated. It is not only style: a final class whose stored properties are all `let` of Sendable type gets `Sendable` conformance for free, which matters as soon as the value crosses an actor boundary.

question: What are optionals in Swift and how do you safely unwrap them?
answer:
An optional makes "this value might be missing" part of the type instead of a runtime surprise.

Under the hood `Optional<T>` is an enum with two cases, `.some(T)` and `.none`, which you write in source as `T?`.

Safe unwrapping options:
• `if let` / `guard let` — bind only when non-nil; the shorthand `guard let name else` reuses the same name
• `??` — nil-coalescing default
• `?.` — optional chaining, propagates nil through the whole expression
• `map` / `flatMap` — transform the wrapped value without unwrapping
• `switch` on `.some` / `.none` when you want both branches explicit

Force-unwrapping with `!` traps on nil. Reserve it for cases that are genuinely unreachable — a hardcoded URL literal, an outlet the storyboard guarantees — and write a real error path everywhere else. `try!` and implicitly unwrapped optionals (`String!`) carry the same risk.

question: Explain value types vs reference types in Swift.
answer:
Swift divides every type into value types, which are copied when you assign or pass them, and reference types, which are shared.

• Value types — struct, enum, tuple. Each variable owns its own copy, so nobody else can mutate it behind your back. That is what makes them the safe default under strict concurrency.
• Reference types — class, actor, closure. Many variables can point at one instance, and a mutation through any of them is visible to all.

Apple's guidance is to reach for `struct` first and use `class` only when you need something a value cannot give you: stable identity (`===`), inheritance, `deinit`, or Objective-C bridging.

The standard library collections — Array, Dictionary, Set, String — are all value types with copy-on-write. The buffer is shared until someone writes to it, so a copy costs a retain, not a memcpy. `isKnownUniquelyReferenced` is how you implement the same trick in your own types.

question: What are closures in Swift and how do capture lists work?
answer:
Closures are self-contained blocks of functionality (named or anonymous) that can be passed around. They capture variables from their surrounding scope by reference (for reference types) or by copying (for value types).

A capture list `[weak self]` / `[unowned self]` lets you opt into different memory semantics — required to avoid retain cycles when a closure outlives its owner (e.g. stored on a view, networking layer, or NotificationCenter).

Trailing-closure syntax + shorthand parameters ($0, $1) make Swift closures concise.

question: What is the difference between Array, Set, and Dictionary in Swift?
answer:
Array, Set and Dictionary are the three standard-library collections, and choosing between them is really a choice about ordering and lookup cost.

• `Array<Element>` — ordered and index-addressed, duplicates allowed. O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, but O(n) for `contains`.
• `Set<Element>` — unordered and unique; `Element` must be `Hashable`. O(1) average insert and `contains`, plus union/intersection/subtracting.
• `Dictionary<Key, Value>` — unordered key-to-value pairs with unique `Hashable` keys. O(1) average lookup.

All three are value types with copy-on-write, so passing one around is cheap until somebody mutates it.

All three also conform to Sequence and Collection, so `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sorted` and `first(where:)` work identically on each — which is why the right answer to "my `contains` is slow in a loop" is usually "turn the Array into a Set first".

question: Explain Swift error handling: throws, try, do/catch, Result.
answer:
Swift makes failure part of a function's signature: a function that can fail is marked `throws` and every caller must write `try`.

Errors are ordinary values conforming to the `Error` protocol, and an enum with associated values is the usual shape — it lets the caller `switch` on the exact failure and pull out a retry delay or a field name.

Forms of try:
• `try` — propagate the error to the caller
• `try?` — collapse to an Optional, discarding the error
• `try!` — trap on error; same risk profile as force-unwrapping

`do` / `catch` handles the error locally, and `catch` patterns can match specific cases. When you need to store an outcome rather than handle it immediately — caching, passing across a boundary, testing — use `Result<Success, Failure>`.

Typed throws (`func f() throws(AuthError)`) landed in Swift 6: the compiler then knows the exact error type, so `catch` is exhaustive and no `as?` cast is needed. Untyped `throws` is still the default and still right for most APIs, because adding a new error case to a typed throws function is a source-breaking change.

question: Swift has tuples, ranges and `guard` — what problem does each one solve?
answer:
Tuples, ranges and `guard` are three small features that turn up in almost every Swift file, and each one replaces something heavier.

• Tuple — a fixed-size group of typed, optionally named values. It buys you a multi-value return without declaring a struct: `func minMax(_ xs: [Int]) -> (min: Int, max: Int)?`. The moment the tuple escapes the function it was made in, or needs a method, promote it to a struct.
• Range — `0..<10` is half-open, `1...10` is closed, and one-sided forms like `2...` and `...2` slice collections. Ranges conform to Sequence, so you iterate them directly and use them as subscripts into arrays and strings.
• guard — an early exit that the compiler forces you to honour: the `else` block must leave the current scope. Unlike `if let`, the bound value stays in scope for the rest of the function, so the happy path stays flat and unindented instead of drifting right with every nested check.

The rule of thumb for `guard` versus `if let`: use `guard` when the nil case means "we're done here", and `if let` when the nil case is just another branch you want to handle.

question: Why does Swift refuse to let you write name[3] on a String, and what is a Substring?
answer:
A Swift Character is an extended grapheme cluster — what a reader calls one character — and clusters take different amounts of memory, so there is no constant-time way to jump to the fourth one.

That single fact explains the whole API:
• Indices are opaque. You get one by walking: `startIndex`, `index(after:)`, `index(_:offsetBy:)`, `firstIndex(of:)`, and an index from one string is meaningless in another.
• `count` is a walk too, so it costs O(n). Use `isEmpty` rather than comparing the count to zero.
• Comparison is by canonical equivalence, so an accented letter typed as one scalar equals the same letter typed as letter plus combining mark, even though the byte counts differ.
• When you need fixed-width units there are views for that: `unicodeScalars`, `utf8`, `utf16`.

A Substring is what slicing gives you — `s.prefix(5)`, `s.split(separator:)`, `s[range]`. It shares the parent's storage instead of copying, which makes slicing cheap, but it also keeps that whole parent alive. Convert with `String(sub)` before you store it somewhere long-lived, and take the copy consciously: that is the moment the memory is actually allocated.

Everyday tools that avoid index arithmetic entirely: `hasPrefix`, `contains`, `replacingOccurrences`, `split`, `joined`, interpolation, and multi-line literals.

question: You have an array of optional strings and want the lengths of the ones that exist. map, compactMap or flatMap?
answer:
compactMap is the one that transforms and drops the nils in a single pass, and it is the answer here.

The four together:
• `map` — one output per input, same order, same count. Over `[String?]` it hands you `[Int?]`, which just moves the problem.
• `compactMap` — apply the transform, then discard every nil result. That is how `[String?]` becomes `[Int]`, and it is also the idiomatic way to parse a list where some entries are bad, because `Int(text)` returns an optional.
• `flatMap` — the transform returns a sequence and the results are concatenated one level deep, turning `[[Int]]` into `[Int]`. The optional-flattening overload was renamed to compactMap years ago, so seeing `flatMap` on optionals means old code.
• `reduce` — fold everything into one value. Use `reduce(into:)` when the accumulator is an array, set or dictionary, so it is mutated in place instead of copied on every step.

Two things worth saying out loud in an interview. These chains are eager, so each stage allocates its own array; adding `.lazy` at the front makes them fuse into one pass, which matters when the chain is long or you only take a prefix. And `filter` followed by `map` is two passes doing what one `compactMap` does.

question: What can Swift's switch do that a C-style switch cannot?
answer:
It matches patterns rather than integer values, the compiler forces it to be exhaustive, and no case ever falls through by accident.

What you can switch on:
• Enum cases, binding their associated values in the same breath
• Ranges, including one-sided ones
• Tuples, so two conditions are matched together instead of nested
• Types, with `case let x as SomeType`
• Optionals, strings, and anything you teach it through the pattern-match operator

Extras that change how you write code:
• A `where` clause refines a case, so the branch reads as one condition instead of a case plus an `if` inside it.
• Exhaustiveness is checked for enums you own — add a case and every switch that forgot it stops compiling, which is the main reason to model state as an enum. For enums from a library that may grow, `@unknown default` keeps you compiling while still warning when a new case appears.
• Fallthrough is opt-in with the `fallthrough` keyword, and an empty case is a compile error rather than an accidental fall-through, so you write `break` when you truly mean nothing.
• When you only care about one shape, `if case`, `guard case` and `for case let` give you the same pattern matching without a whole switch.

question: What does inout actually do, and how is it different from passing a class instance?
answer:
An inout parameter is copy-in, copy-out: the function works on a mutable copy and the value is written back over your variable when the call returns.

Consequences that follow from that definition:
• The call site needs an ampersand and a mutable storage location — a `var`, a property, an array element. A `let` or a literal will not compile, and the ampersand is there so the mutation is visible to whoever reads the code.
• It is not a C pointer. The optimiser may pass an address, but semantically the write-back happens at return, so you cannot assume another thread or another closure sees the intermediate writes.
• Exclusive access is enforced. Handing the same variable to two inout parameters is rejected, sometimes at compile time and otherwise by a runtime trap, because the two write-backs would race.
• It cannot escape. You may not capture an inout parameter in an escaping closure or store it for later; there would be nothing to write back to.
• A `mutating` method on a struct is exactly this feature applied to self.

Passing a class instance is a different thing entirely: the reference is copied, both sides point at the same object, and mutating its properties is visible everywhere immediately with no ampersand in sight. Marking a class parameter inout says something narrower — that the function may repoint your variable at a different object.

Style: prefer returning a new value. Reach for inout for in-place algorithms and for large buffers where copying is the actual cost.

question: What is the difference between is, as?, as! and a plain as?
answer:
Three of them ask a question about a value's real type at runtime, while a plain `as` is an upcast the compiler already knows is safe.

• `is` — a Bool test: does this value have that dynamic type, or conform to that protocol
• `as?` — a conditional downcast that yields an optional, so it pairs naturally with `if let` and `guard let`
• `as!` — the same downcast, forced; it traps the process when the value is not what you claimed, exactly like a force unwrap
• `as` with no punctuation — a conversion the compiler can prove: upcasting a subclass to its superclass or a concrete type to a protocol it conforms to, plus literal and bridging conversions

The two erased container types go with them. `Any` holds absolutely anything, including structs, enums and functions. `AnyObject` holds only class instances, which is why identity comparison, weak references and Objective-C interop are expressed in terms of it.

Where you meet this for real: values pulled out of `[String: Any]` from JSONSerialization, `UserDefaults.object(forKey:)`, notification userInfo, and older Objective-C APIs. In new code, a Codable model or a generic beats a chain of casts, and a `switch` with `case let x as Type` reads better than a ladder of conditional casts. Frequent force casts are a design smell, not a shortcut.
